messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Vannak had spent most of his adult life on the Gulf, leaving before dawn to work the shrimp boats and returning home salt-stiff and tired to the small house he shared with his wife. The event he returned to in his mind was not an injury to himself, but the day his younger brother was lost at sea. They had been working nearby boats in rough weather, the sky gone suddenly hard and metallic, the water chopping in a way every fisherman knows can turn dangerous fast. He remembered the radio breaking up, the shouted fragments, the sight of his brother’s vessel pitching at an angle that looked wrong. By the time help reached him, his brother was gone. Vannak had lived with the fact that he was close enough to hear panic in his brother’s voice and still could not bring him back.

In the months afterward, what settled in him most strongly was not grief alone but a corrosive conclusion about what survival meant. He had come to believe there was something wrong in the simple fact that he was the one who made it home. Sitting at his kitchen table while his brother’s place stayed empty at family gatherings, he felt ashamed to be eating dinner, ashamed to be sleeping under a roof, ashamed each time he stepped onto a boat and earned money from the same water that had taken his brother. Alongside that guilt was a hardening view of other people. The men at the docks who said, “That’s the sea,” sounded to him cold and false; even well-meant reassurances felt hollow. He began to think people could not be trusted to mean what they said or to protect anyone when it mattered. At times he described himself to his wife as feeling “already gone,” as if some part of him had shut down with his brother’s death.

Those beliefs sharpened the sense of danger he carried in his body. On the docks, the crackle of a marine radio or the sudden rev of an engine could send a surge through him so fast that his chest tightened and his hands trembled before he had fully registered why. If the wind picked up or the water slapped hard against the hull, he was overtaken by dread and anger in the same instant. What frightened him most was how immediate it felt: not like remembering, but like his body had decided the worst was happening again. Because he was certain survival had come at his brother’s expense and that no one around him could really be relied upon, he moved through ordinary work as if catastrophe were always close. Nights were no relief. He lay awake listening for weather reports, replaying the broken radio calls, unable to settle into sleep because some part of him stayed braced.

That constant state of alarm, in turn, deepened the way he judged himself and other people. After a day on the boat spent flinching at engine noise and swallowing waves of fear, he would come home convinced this proved he was not the same man anymore. He told himself that a man who had survived when his brother did not had no right to feel weak as well. The physical jolts and the sleepless nights became evidence, in his mind, that he was empty inside now, just going through motions. When his wife tried to sit with him after dinner or asked what he was thinking, he often gave little back. Her concern did not feel comforting; it made him pull further away, more certain that closeness was unsafe because people either failed you or left you. The more his body reacted at work and the less he slept, the more fixed these beliefs became.

Over the past year the pattern tightened around his daily life. He still went out on the water because fishing was the only work he had ever known, but he kept to himself on the boat and watched the men around him warily. At the marina he avoided lingering conversations, suspicious of easy talk and resentful of anyone who joked about storms. At home he sat for long stretches in silence, not exactly sad in a way he could describe, but numb, as if he were sealed off from his own family. His wife finally persuaded him to seek help after several nights when he barely slept at all and then came in from work shaking after hearing a distress call over the radio. What he is most afraid of is that this is permanent—that he survived only to become someone cold, guilty, and always on guard. What he is hoping, though he says it carefully, is to sleep without bracing for disaster and to be with his wife without feeling like he has already disappeared.
